 singapore Project Wolbachia turns 10: Dengue cases in Tampines fell from 1,200 in 2020 to 77 in 2025
 Project now covers 840,000 or 53 per cent, of all Singapore households Wolbachia-Aedes mosquitoes do not bite or spread diseases, and their release helps to reduce dengue risk. PHOTO: AsiaOne/Jasper Lim PUBLISHED ON October 31, 2026 11:00 AM BY Sean Ler Project Wolbachia took a walk down memory lane on Saturday (Oct 31), returning to where it began a decade ago — in Tampines — as the initiative commemorates its 10th year.
 Singapore is the first in the world to deploy the Wolbachia technology in a high-rise, high-density tropical environment for the suppression of the Aedes aegypti mosquito population.
 It began in 2016 at three pilot sites - Braddell Heights, Tampines West and Nee Soon East - and now covers over 840,000, or about 53 per cent, of all households in the country.
 Explaining the project, the National Environment Agency (NEA) said in a media factsheet that when male Wolbachia-Aedes mosquitos mate with urban female Aedes aegypti mosquitos that do not carry Wolbachia, the resulting eggs do not hatch.
 This, in turn, reduces the Aedes aegypti mosquito population by up to 90 per cent at release sites, with residents in those areas experiencing over 70 per cent reduction in dengue risk.
 The male Wolbachia-Aedes mosquitoes do not bite or spread diseases.
 Speaking at a commemorative event in Tampines West on Saturday, Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment Dr Janil Puthucheary noted that the reduction in dengue risk was published in The New England Journal of Medicine, one of the world's leading medical journals, earlier this year.
 More importantly, he said, the reduction in dengue risk among residents in the deployment areas is a significant step forward in efforts to protect communities from dengue.
 The senior minister of state pointed out that dengue cases in Tampines has also fallen from almost 1,200 during a major outbreak in 2020, to just 77 cases last year.
 "Of course, dengue cases fluctuate from year to year, but this is an encouraging sign that our sustained efforts to protect our communities are making a very real difference," he said, adding that the decade-long project has seen local and international scientists and institutions partnering it to further innovative technologies, processes and operational capabilities.
 But he also cautioned that Project Wolbachia is not a silver bullet and does not replace the need for communities and residents to remain vigilant, adding that dengue prevention is a shared responsibility.
 "We must continue to do our part to keep our homes and neighbourhoods free of mosquito breeding sites, so that we can sustain the progress we have made."
 Meanwhile, the World Health Organisation is reviewing scientific evidence on Wolbachia approaches, including lessons from Singapore, to develop future guidance for countries.
 What began as just an experimental research project has since grown into an important public health intervention, with the potential to benefit communities well beyond our shores.
